summary.lead: Official summary (Congressional Research Service, Passed Senate):

blocks.text: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026
This bill modifies federal permitting processes to expedite a wide range of projects. It also excludes from federal income tax certain damages from lawsuits relating to sexual acts.
The bill limits the scope of the National Environmental Policy Act, including by
further limiting the types of federal actions that trigger environmental review, and
exempting additional types of projects from environmental review.
The bill also limits permit obligations under the Clean Water Act, including by
narrowing the scope of review for water quality certifications,
extending the term for permits issued under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, and
limiting the time period for review of permits for discharges of dredged or fill materials.
It also shortens timelines for certain requirements concerning threatened or endangered species to expedite permits.
Additionally, the bill addresses numerous aspects of energy infrastructure permitting, including by
expanding the authority of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to issue construction permits for certain interstate electricity transmission projects;
directing FERC to establish ratepayer protections related to certain large computational loads (e.g. data centers);
removing permit requirements for onshore oil and gas drilling on nonfederal land; and
accelerating renewable energy, geothermal, hydropower, nuclear, or offshore energy projects.
It also limits the types of projects that trigger review under the National Historic Preservation Act.
Finally, the bill excludes from an individual's federal income tax certain damages received due to sexual acts or contact, regardless of whether there are medical records or observable injuries.

This bill speeds up approval of many federal projects by cutting back several environmental and historic review rules. It also says that certain money damages from lawsuits over sexual acts are not taxed as federal income.

On environmental reviews, the bill narrows the National Environmental Policy Act. It reduces the kinds of federal actions that require an environmental review and exempts some additional types of projects from that review.

The bill also loosens some permit requirements under the Clean Water Act. It narrows the review for state water quality certifications, extends the length of certain pollution discharge permits issued under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, and sets a shorter time limit for reviewing permits for discharging dredged or fill materials into waters.

It shortens some timelines for rules protecting threatened or endangered species, so that permits can be issued faster. In addition, it changes several parts of energy permitting. It lets the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issue construction permits for certain interstate electricity transmission lines, and it directs that agency to set protections for ratepayers related to large computing facilities such as data centers. The bill also removes permit requirements for onshore oil and gas drilling on non-federal land and speeds up projects involving renewable, geothermal, hydropower, nuclear, or offshore energy.

Finally, the bill limits which projects must go through review under the National Historic Preservation Act. It also provides that damages an individual receives from sexual acts or contact are excluded from federal income tax, whether or not there are medical records or visible injuries.
